mcqs.question: A problem states its constraint as n <= 20. What is that constraint most likely signaling about the intended approach?
options: That the intended solution is O(n log n) and the bound is unrelated to complexity
That an O(n^3) polynomial algorithm is expected, since 20 is a small number
That a linear scan is sufficient regardless of the rest of the problem
That an approach exponential in n, such as enumerating all 2^n subsets or a bitmask DP, is intended and fits the time budget
mcqs.explanation: n <= 20 keeps 2^n around a million, which is exactly the scale where bitmask enumeration or bitmask DP is both intended and fast enough — interviewers use small-n bounds specifically to signal exponential-in-n approaches are safe. A bound that small would be an unusually restrictive way to hint at a polynomial or linear algorithm, which typically tolerate far larger n.

mcqs.question: In `for mask in range(1 << n): ...` followed by an inner loop checking each of the n bit positions, what is the overall time complexity of enumerating all subsets this way?
options: O(2^n), since checking bits is treated as free
O(n^2), since there are two nested loops
O(n), since bitwise operations run in constant time
O(n * 2^n), since there are 2^n masks and each one costs O(n) to decode
mcqs.explanation: There are 2^n masks total, and decoding each mask into its member items costs O(n) for the inner loop over bit positions, giving O(n * 2^n) overall. Bitwise operations being fast doesn't make the outer loop free, and O(n) or O(n^2) both undercount the exponential outer loop.

mcqs.question: In the submask-enumeration loop `sub = (sub - 1) & mask`, what does ANDing with `mask` accomplish that subtracting 1 alone would not?
options: It reverses the order in which submasks are produced
It clips the result back down to only the bit positions mask actually has set, so the walk stays within mask's own submasks rather than drifting into unrelated bits
It converts sub into the complement of mask
It is redundant and included only for readability
mcqs.explanation: Subtracting 1 alone borrows through trailing zeros the same way n & (n-1) does, but it can set bits that mask itself doesn't have; ANDing with mask discards those, guaranteeing every value produced is a genuine submask of mask. It isn't reversing order or producing a complement, and it isn't redundant — removing it breaks correctness.

mcqs.question: Given two subsets represented as masks, mask1 and mask2, which expression computes their set difference (items in mask1 but not in mask2)?
options: mask1 & ~mask2
mask1 | mask2
mask1 & mask2
mask1 ^ mask2
mcqs.explanation: mask1 & ~mask2 keeps only the bits present in mask1 while excluding anything present in mask2, which is exactly set difference. mask1 | mask2 is the union, mask1 & mask2 is the intersection, and mask1 ^ mask2 is the symmetric difference (items in exactly one of the two sets, not the one-directional difference asked for).

mcqs.question: In a bitmask DP for the traveling salesman problem, dp[mask][i] represents the minimum cost of a route visiting exactly the cities in mask and ending at city i. What does transitioning from dp[mask][i] to dp[mask | (1 << j)][j] represent?
options: Removing city j from the route entirely
Recomputing dp[mask][i] from scratch for a different starting city
Extending the route by visiting an unvisited city j next, arriving from city i
Checking whether city j was ever visited in any route
mcqs.explanation: mask | (1 << j) adds city j to the visited set, and the new state's cost adds the edge cost from i to j — exactly the effect of extending the current route by one more stop at j. It doesn't remove anything (that would be a clear operation, not OR), and it isn't a from-scratch recomputation or a pure membership check.

mcqs.question: A problem has n = 45 items and asks for an optimal subset under some constraint. Why is a bitmask DP over all 2^n subsets not a viable approach here?
options: Bitmask DP only works when n is odd
2^45 is far too large to enumerate or store a DP table over within any realistic time or memory budget, so a different algorithmic approach is needed
Bitmasks longer than 32 bits are not supported in any programming language
The DP transitions would require floating-point arithmetic at this scale
mcqs.explanation: 2^45 is on the order of 3.5 * 10^13 — vastly beyond what any per-mask work, however cheap, can process in a reasonable time budget, and a dp table of that size doesn't fit in memory either. Bitmask parity, language bit-width limits (most languages support 64-bit or arbitrary-precision integers), and floating-point arithmetic are unrelated to why this fails.
